tasks.title: Passage 1
tasks.instructions: Read the passage and choose the correct answers. /4 x 2 = 8 points/
tasks.text:
For thousands of years, people had to find ways to keep food from going bad. Before the invention of the refrigerator, families dried meat and fish in the sun, or preserved vegetables with salt. In cold countries, people cut large blocks of ice from frozen lakes in winter and stored **them** in underground rooms covered with straw. The ice could last until late summer, but it was heavy, expensive and difficult to transport.

In the 1800s, inventors began to experiment with machines that could produce cold air. The first home refrigerators appeared in the early twentieth century, but they were large, noisy and very costly. Only wealthy families could afford one. By the 1950s, however, factories were producing them in large numbers, and prices fell <u>sharply</u>.

The refrigerator changed far more than the kitchen. Because food stayed fresh for longer, people no longer needed to shop every day. Supermarkets grew larger, and farmers could send fresh products to distant cities. Today it is hard to imagine a home without a refrigerator, yet it has been common for less than a hundred years.

Our hotel is small but comfortable, and the staff are very friendly. 39. _________ we tried Korean barbecue for the first time, and Nara ate so much that she could hardly walk back to the hotel!

tasks.title: Listening
tasks.instructions: You are going to listen to a woman interviewing a student. Read each question and choose the correct answer. You have 1 minute and 30 seconds to look through the questions before you listen. You will listen to the passage twice only, so listen carefully. /6 x 2 = 12 points/
tasks.audioScript:
Interviewer: Good afternoon. I'm writing an article for the university magazine about students who do volunteer work. Can I ask you a few questions?
Student: Sure, no problem.
Interviewer: First, could you tell me your name?
Student: It's Anna Delgado. That's D-E-L-G-A-D-O.
Interviewer: Thank you. So, Anna, what kind of volunteer work do you do?
Student: I help at an animal shelter near the city centre. I feed the dogs, clean their cages and take them for walks.
Interviewer: How often do you go there?
Student: At the moment, about twice a week, usually on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Last year I went almost every day, but now I have a part-time job in a bookshop, so I don't have as much time.
Interviewer: Do you do anything else in your free time?
Student: I play volleyball for the university team, and I sometimes paint, although I'm not very good at it.
Interviewer: Why did you start volunteering?
Student: Well, I've always loved animals, but we live in a small flat, so my family can't keep a pet. Volunteering is the next best thing.
Interviewer: And what are your plans for the future?
Student: I'd like to study veterinary medicine after I finish my degree in biology.
Interviewer: And what are you doing after this interview?
Student: I'm going straight to the shelter. A new group of puppies arrived this morning!
Interviewer: Well, thank you, Anna, and good luck.
